first.rationale: The objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, so verification capacity goes to the two inherited beliefs that are simultaneously most decision-critical and most weakly supported *for that objective*. memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the belief that most directly tempts the obvious response to the competitor's entry pricing, and its recorded support is acquisition and revenue lift — measures that say nothing about margin durability, cohort quality, or retention of discount-acquired accounts; if that record turns out to be short-window or acquisition-only, the whole pricing direction collapses under the stated objective. memory_86 (shortened onboarding) is the belief I currently intend to act on and it is supported only by proxy outcomes (completion rate, time-to-value, early adoption) rather than qualified revenue, so it is exactly the kind of consequential-but-under-supported claim the triage invariant targets. I did not spend budget on memory_57 (referral) because it already carries a revenue-and-retention-linked result and is better supported for this objective, nor on memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist), which is well-specified but addresses a segment unrelated to the two observed regressions, nor on memory_31/memory_91, which are adjacent to and partially redundant with memory_86. Current intent: simplify_onboarding, run as a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout. Reasoning: the two internal regressions (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%) are real, measurable, and internally caused, whereas the competitor pricing pressure invites a discount response whose revenue is likely to be lower-quality and margin-eroding — a poor fit for 'sustainable.' But I hold this loosely: the entire evidentiary basis for onboarding simplification is funnel proxies, and proxy improvement has a well-known failure mode of pulling in accounts that complete onboarding without ever converting to qualified revenue, or of cutting signup fields that were actually doing qualification work. That downstream risk is why the scale is guarded and why revenue-quality guardrails (not just completion rate) should be the read-out. If the memory_86 archive shows the original lift was measured only at the completion/adoption layer with no revenue follow-through, or was run on a non-comparable cohort, I would downgrade to a narrower diagnostic or shift toward activation_messaging; if the memory_73 archive unexpectedly shows durable retained revenue from discounted cohorts, promotional pricing becomes defensible as a direct competitive response.

mid.rationale: Both verifications paid off, and in opposite directions. exp_73 falsifies the load-bearing part of memory_73: the +31% signup and +18% qualified revenue were real but the cohort carried -12% 30-day retention and did not survive first renewal. The archived record contains an explicit instruction not to generalize targeted discounting as sustainable growth. Under a primary objective of *sustainable* long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is now ruled out for this slot, notwithstanding that it is the most direct-seeming answer to the competitor's entry pricing. This is exactly the trap the consolidated memory had smoothed over: the one-line summary preserved the revenue lift and dropped the retention collapse. I am treating the competitor pressure as a condition to be survived on product quality rather than matched on price. exp_86 confirms memory_86 and, importantly, resolves the specific weakness I flagged before verifying: the effect is not proxy-only. Completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days are accompanied by 30-day retention +3%, so the funnel improvement carries a positive rather than dilutive quality signal, which is the failure mode I was worried about (pulling in accounts that complete onboarding but never become qualified revenue). That upgrade in evidentiary quality is what moves me from a small guarded test to a standard experiment. It also aligns with the strongest situational fit: onboarding completion is down 4% and activation is down 6% quarter over quarter, both internally caused and both directly addressed by this lever, with memory_31 and memory_91 pointing the same way on activation. Residual uncertainty I am not papering over: exp_86's retention read is 30-day, which is shorter than the renewal-cycle horizon on which exp_73's discount cohort actually failed, so a +3% 30-day figure does not by itself establish durability at renewal. I also do not know whether the original exp_86 cohort resembles today's population under active competitive poaching, or whether the current 4% completion decline shares a cause with the flow exp_86 shortened. So the experiment should read out on qualified-revenue and renewal-horizon retention guardrails, not completion rate alone, and should be reversible. If activation fails to recover, activation_messaging (memory_91) is the next lever; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) remains well-supported but targets a segment unrelated to either observed regression, and referral_incentive (memory_57) is better held until the activation base is repaired, since referrals amplify an intake funnel that is currently underperforming.

final2.rationale: The deeper price cut and doubled churn conversations raise urgency but do not change the evidence, and urgency is precisely the condition under which the discount lever gets adopted on vibes. exp_73 is the one thing I verified with hard numbers this cycle: +31% signup, +18% qualified revenue, -12% 30-day retention, with the source record explicitly warning against generalizing targeted discounting as sustainable growth. Matching a competitor's second cut would buy visible short-term relief and, on the only direct evidence I have, hand back a cohort that does not survive first renewal — the opposite of the stated primary objective. Spending the single non-carryover slot there would also consume the week on the lever I have the most reason to distrust. I want to name a real gap rather than overclaim: exp_73 tested *acquisition* discounting on new price-sensitive SMB signups. Today's problem is partly different — retention pricing or save-offers aimed at *existing* accounts already in churn conversations. That is a genuinely distinct mechanism and exp_73 does not directly falsify it; an existing account with established usage and time-to-value may behave nothing like a discount-acquired one. So my position is not 'pricing is proven bad,' it is 'the only pricing evidence I hold is adverse, the retention-pricing variant is unverified, and an unverified variant is not a good use of the one irreversible slot in the week I cannot check it.' That question is my first archive pull next week. Holding simplify_onboarding, standard scale. It is the only direction where I have verified end-to-end support including a positive retention signal (completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%), it addresses the two internally caused regressions actually visible in the data (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and faster time-to-value is a defensible answer to price pressure: accounts that reach value quickly are less winnable by a cheaper competitor. Retention pressure at renewal is a value problem before it is a price problem. Uncertainty I am carrying: exp_86's retention read is 30-day, shorter than the renewal horizon on which the discount cohort actually failed, and its cohort predates active poaching, so durability under current conditions is not established. This will not stop churn conversations this week, and I should say that to leadership plainly rather than imply otherwise. Guardrails: read out on qualified revenue and renewal-horizon retention, not completion rate; keep the change reversible; track price-attributed churn separately so next week's decision has a clean signal. Non-experiment save motions for at-risk accounts can run through normal account management without consuming the experiment slot.
